Modified response using the SLOOS as context:
- The statement acknowledges severe, pandemic-driven declines in activity, jobs, and inflation. The April 2020 Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey (SLOOS) indicates broad-based tightening in bank credit that reinforces this weakness: banks tightened standards and terms on C&I loans to firms of all sizes (including wider spreads and higher premiums), and on commercial real estate—particularly multifamily—with tighter LTVs and covenants. Many consumer categories, including HELOCs and credit cards, also saw tighter standards. Foreign banks reported similar tightening.
- SLOOS cites the deteriorating economic outlook, reduced risk tolerance, liquidity concerns, and COVID-19-specific factors (including supervisory/legislative/accounting changes) as key reasons for tighter standards. Demand was mixed: firms showed stronger near-term borrowing needs tied to liquidity and credit line usage, while demand for CRE/multifamily weakened.
- Implication: Despite the Fed’s near-zero rates, continued Treasury/agency MBS/CMBS purchases, and repo operations aimed at improving market functioning, the tightening of bank lending standards highlighted by SLOOS suggests constrained credit supply will weigh on the recovery and dampen transmission of accommodative policy in the near term.

Net effect: sentiment remains clearly negative and somewhat more adverse than when judged on market-functioning improvements alone, given credit supply constraints indicated by SLOOS.
